EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong surface low pressure system moved through the Great Lakes region, with a tight pressure gradient existing between it and a surface high departing off the eastern United States coast. This pressure gradient led to strong, gusty winds over the area, especially across the higher elevations. During the day of January 29th, a west-northwesterly low level jet also moved eastward into the Piedmont, and contributed to more strengthening of the winds. Wind gusts of 60 mph and greater resulted in a few hundred power outages in the northwest North Carolina mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 71 mph gust was measured at the Ashe County Airport, and a 69 mph gust was measured near Baldwin. Over 720 customers in Ashe County had lost power by the morning of January 29.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level storm system tracked across the eastern United States through the day of January 11 and into the overnight, while the resultant surface low moved from the Gulf Coast into the Carolina coast. Some initial precipitation spread over North Carolina from the surface low, but the heavier precipitation occurred with the passage of the upper level storm system. Strong lift resulted in some banding of heavy snow with localized areas of higher accumulations of northwest North Carolina. The accumulating snow led to hazardous road conditions and some vehicle accidents, a few of which resulted in road closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level storm system moved southeast through the Rockies, then east across the Southern U.S. on January 21-22. This storm system overlapped with an usually cold airmass already in place across much of the U.S., leading to a rare deep south winter storm that blanketed Eastern North Carolina with at least several inches of snow. Snow began during the evening hours of the 21st as a surface trough moved into the Coastal Plain with snowfall then spreading east as the evening progressed and a stationary front set up offshore. Snow became heavy at times especially across portions of the Outer Banks where the highest snowfall amounts fell. Snow then quickly ended across the Coastal Plain on the morning of the 22nd while snow stuck around the OBX and eastern Carteret County until the afternoon on the 22nd. The winter storm was responsible for producing a swath of 2-6 of snow for much of ENC, with several locations across the Outer Banks reporting amounts as high as 6-9.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread public reports of six to nine inches of snowfall. Snow fell between the evening of the 21st and the morning of the 22nd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level storm system moved southeast through the Rockies, then east across the Southern U.S. on January 21-22. This storm system overlapped with an usually cold airmass already in place across much of the U.S., leading to a rare deep south winter storm that blanketed Eastern North Carolina with at least several inches of snow. Snow began during the evening hours of the 21st as a surface trough moved into the Coastal Plain with snowfall then spreading east as the evening progressed and a stationary front set up offshore. Snow became heavy at times especially across portions of the Outer Banks where the highest snowfall amounts fell. Snow then quickly ended across the Coastal Plain on the morning of the 22nd while snow stuck around the OBX and eastern Carteret County until the afternoon on the 22nd. The winter storm was responsible for producing a swath of 2-6 of snow for much of ENC, with several locations across the Outer Banks reporting amounts as high as 6-9.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread reports of three to five inches of snow fell across northern Craven County between the evening of the 21st and the morning of the 22nd.

Total accumulations were generally 3-6 inches across the high elevations along the Tennessee border. Lower elevations northwest of a line from the Pigeon River drainage through far northern Buncombe County through the northern mountains received anywhere from 0.5 inch up to 2 inches with locally higher amounts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NA

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, the center of a strong arctic high (1040mb) extending from the central CONUS to the East Coast gradually moved from the Mississippi Valley on January 21 to the East Coast on January 22. Meanwhile, an area of low pressure formed in central Gulf along a stationary front extending from the central Gulf to offshore of the East Coast. Aloft, a sharpening but positively tiled shortwave trough crossed the area during the evening of the January 21 through the early morning of January 22. A very cold and dry low-level Arctic airmass was in place over the entire area with temperatures in the lower-mid 20s (with dew points around 0F) during the afternoon on January 22 before any snow had started to fall. Even though the surface low tracked well to the southeast of the area, mid to upper level forcing for ascent was strong given decent warm air advection aloft. The sloping mid to upper level frontogenesis zone was over the area, with the strongest frontogenesis in the dendritic growth zone (700-550mb) residing over southeast Virginia during the evening into early overnight hours on January 21. Despite the very cold and dry antecedent airmass, light snow began falling as far west as the Richmond Metro by 7 PM. The low-levels then quickly saturated area-wide by 8-9 PM. Most of the snow was light in intensity, but a band of moderate to heavy snow (likely with 1-2���/hour rates) set up across extreme southeast Virginia and northeast North Carolina on the warm side of the mid-level frontogenesis zone. In addition, given the very cold temperatures (and forcing for ascent concentrated in the dendritic growth zone), snow-to-liquid ratios were 15-20:1 even across northeast North Carolina. Also, given the cold low-level temperatures (925mb temperatures of -13 to -16C) and the northerly flow, some additional enhancement of the snow was observed across Norfolk into portions of interior northeast North Carolina due to moisture flow off the bay. The steady snow ended between midnight and 4 AM on January 22 as the shortwave quickly pushed offshore, but totals across northeast North Carolina ranged from 3-7 inches (locally 8 inches). Southern portions of Hampton Roads saw around 3 inches, with localized totals around 4 inches in that area of Norfolk that saw bay-enhanced snow. After the steady synoptic snow ended, a bay-effect snow band developed given minimal shear from the surface to 900mb (with the top of that layer in the dendritic growth zone). In addition, the difference between the water temperature (38F/3C) and the 900mb temperature (around -15C) was more than enough for a few hundred J/kg of bay-induced instability. This combination of factors set the stage for a true bay effect snow event that likely produced localized snow totals of 0.5 inches on top of what had already fallen. The bay effect band drifted west and weakened by 5-6 AM as the fetch over the bay was disrupted with the low-level flow shifting from due north to north-northeast. However, another band of bay-effect snow showers developed from late morning into the afternoon on January 22 near the Norfolk area before tapering off.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals generally ranged from 3 to 5 inches across Gates County. A snowfall total of 5 inches was reported 2 miles (SW) from Easons Crossroads.

Southern portions of Hampton Roads saw around 3 inches, with localized totals around 4 inches in that area of Norfolk that saw bay-enhanced snow. After the steady synoptic snow ended, a bay-effect snow band developed given minimal shear from the surface to 900mb (with the top of that layer in the dendritic growth zone). In addition, the difference between the water temperature (38F/3C) and the 900mb temperature (around -15C) was more than enough for a few hundred J/kg of bay-induced instability. This combination of factors set the stage for a true bay effect snow event that likely produced localized snow totals of 0.5 inches on top of what had already fallen. The bay effect band drifted west and weakened by 5-6 AM as the fetch over the bay was disrupted with the low-level flow shifting from due north to north-northeast. However, another band of bay-effect snow showers developed from late morning into the afternoon on January 22 near the Norfolk area before tapering off.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm brought numerous impacts to North Carolina Sunday January 5th and into Monday January 6th. A strong surface low pressure system moved northeastward from the Central Plains and into the Tennessee and Ohio Valleys, with the associated warm front lifting northward from the southeast into the lower Mid Atlantic. Precipitation began as snow, but strong warm air advection ahead of the low pressure center, and behind the warm front, led to a transition to all liquid precipitation. Surface temperatures remained below freezing, and so a prolonged period of freezing rain led to ice accumulations up to a quarter of an inch overnight and during the Monday morning commute. Hundreds had lost power by the morning of January 6th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Up to an inch of snow fell across the county from January 5th through January 6th. Between 0.10 and 0.15 inches of ice accumulated as well. Key Impacts: traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation overspread the Carolina mountains and North Carolina foothills during the evening of the 11th in association with an approaching frontal system. While temperatures were above freezing across much of the area, a pocket of cold air developed along the Blue Ridge escarpment, resulting in precipitation falling as freezing rain there for a prolonged period. Total ice accretion was mainly in the 0.10-0.25 range across this area, although some pockets along the continental divide saw more than 0.25 inch, with isolated to scattered power outages reported. Meanwhile, areas across the western halves of Buncombe, Henderson, Yancey, and  Mitchell Counties, and much of the southern half of Caldwell and Alexander Counties only received rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A high pressure wedge was situated over the region as a surface low pressure system developed over the southern Plains, with an expansive area of precipitation that shifted eastward into the Mid Atlantic during the day of February 11. Precipitation began as snow, but with the high pressure wedge in place and warm air increasing aloft, a transition from snow to sleet and freezing rain occurred along and south of the North Carolina and Virginia border. Ice accumulations on trees and power lines resulted in thousands of power outages and road closures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Between 0.15 and 0.75 inches of ice accumulated across Watauga County from February 11 through February 12. The highest amount of 0.75 inches was reported just southeast of Deep Gap. Over 5600 customers were reported without power by the mid afternoon of February 12. Key Impacts: power outages, downed trees, road closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed along the U.S. Gulf Coast, traveled northeast up along the Southeast U.S. coastline, then off the coast of the Carolinas during the time period of February 19th to the early morning hours of February 20th. As this occurred, an area of widespread precipitation developed along the track of the low. Where temperatures were cold enough, there was a mix of sleet, freezing rain, and snow. For areas from the Crystal Coast through the southern Outer Banks, the precipitation type was mostly rain. This event produced a swath of accumulating sleet and snow from central North Carolina through southeast Virginia. South of the snow and sleet, there was a swath of accumulating ice, with a zone of 0.10 - 0.30 of ice accretion. The combination of ice and wind led to tree and power line damage across parts of ENC, with numerous power outages reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A combination of public, trained spotter, and emergency management reported a mix of freezing rain, sleet, and snow impacting the county during the day and into the overnight hours. Widespread snow and sleet reports of two to five inches occurred with freezing rain accumulations of 0.10-0.25 inches noted as well.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Late in the afternoon, a supercell thunderstorm moved into southeast Martin County before moving northeastward through Martin and far western Washington Counties. As the thunderstorm moved through Martin County, a tornado touched down in an open field southwest of Jamesville. In this area, a trained storm spotter captured the touchdown with a drone. The drone footage shows a well-defined low-level mesocyclone and a loosely-organized condensation funnel that touched the ground. The supercell thunderstorm then moved northeast through Jamesville and into far western Washington County. Here there were numerous reports of funnel clouds relayed to the National Weather Service via the county 911 center. It is unknown whether the tornado |touched down at any additional point after the initial touchdown report. Radar data showed strengthening low-level rotation after the initial report, suggesting a high likelihood of additional brief touchdowns. However, there isn't conclusive evidence of |additional touchdowns, and no damage has been reported at any point along the supercell's path.||On rare occasions, it is impossible to rate the strength of a confirmed tornado because this is little to no damage evidence. As of this afternoon(Tuesday May 6th, 2025), this tornado has not produced any confirmed damage therefore per Directive: 10-1605, |this tornado has a rating of EF-U. The start coordinates were estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm occurred over the Mid-Atlantic February 19-20 2025. Arctic 1050mb high pressure built into the area early on the 19th. Two mid level disturbances began to phase over eastern North Carolina with periods of heavy snowfall featuring 1 to 2 inch per hour snowfall rates. Very cold temperatures resulted in mostly snow across the region, though some sleet did mix in near the Albemarle Sound. Snow totals ranged from around 5 inches for areas west of Interstate 95 to 14 inches in Currituck County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall ranged from 6 to 8 inches across the county. The emergency manager measured 8 inches of snow in Harrellsville, NC.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front on the night of March 16 into the early morning hours of March 17 across northeast North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service Storm Survey Team determined that a tornado touched down just southwest of Longview Estates near Woodville Road in Woodville, North Carolina around 302 AM EDT. The tornado quickly moved northeast, rolling and destroying 3 mobile homes in Longview Estates, and damaging several others. Eight injuries occurred in Longview Estates, and the strongest wind speeds of up to 110 mph were in this area. After exiting Longview Estates, the tornado then moved across the Little River and continued into Pasquotank County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very strong S/SE winds developed across the North Carolina mountains early in the morning in advance of a dynamic frontal system. The strongest winds occurred between 3 AM and 5 AM, possibly assisted by a band of rain with embedded heavy showers and isolated thunderstorms that mixed higher winds from aloft to the valley floors. Some minor structural damage was reported to houses across the region, while numerous trees were blown down, some onto structures, vehicles, and power lines. One tree fell on a trailer in the Conestee community of Transylvania County, killing a 13-year-old male and an 11-year-old male who were sleeping inside. Multiple outbuildings were damaged or destroyed in Haywood County. Power outages numbered in the tens of thousands at the peak of the event. The highest reliable measured gust across the area was at the Asheville Regional Airport, where official NWS obs measured a gust of 59 mph at 422 AM. However, damage reports suggest gusts likely reached as high as 70 mph in some locations. The band of showers and storms strengthened as it moved into the Piedmont later in the morning, with a small area of damaging wind gusts developing in northeast Union County in association with a short line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NA

The strongest winds occurred between 3 AM and 5 AM, possibly assisted by a band of rain with embedded heavy showers and isolated thunderstorms that mixed higher winds from aloft to the valley floors. Some minor structural damage was reported to houses across the region, while numerous trees were blown down, some onto structures, vehicles, and power lines. One tree fell on a trailer in the Conestee community of Transylvania County, killing a 13-year-old male and an 11-year-old male who were sleeping inside. Multiple outbuildings were damaged or destroyed in Haywood County. Power outages numbered in the tens of thousands at the peak of the event. The highest reliable measured gust across the area was at the Asheville Regional Airport, where official NWS obs measured a gust of 59 mph at 422 AM. However, damage reports suggest gusts likely reached as high as 70 mph in some locations. The band of showers and storms strengthened as it moved into the Piedmont later in the morning, with a small area of damaging wind gusts developing in northeast Union County in association with a short line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NA

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Southwesterly flow ahead of a cold front across the Ohio Valley increased moisture across the Mid Atlantic, and some clearing allowed CAPE to increase to the 500 to 1000 J/kg range in the Piedmont. However, more cloud cover throughout the morning hindered destabilization somewhat, which limited coverage of storms. Enough shear in the atmosphere did allow some storms to grow stronger, and resulted in some scattered wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees near the intersection of Highway 65 and Easley Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mid to upper level disturbance tracked east across the central and southern Appalachians, coinciding with the peak heating and instability during the afternoon hours. Some storms first developed along the Blue Ridge prior to the convection associated with the upper trough, while storms associated with the trough tracked into the area from the west during the mid to late afternoon. Moderate instability with MUCAPE in the 1000-1500 J/kg, and 0-6km shear was between 35-40 knots, with lapse rate increasing to 7 C/km by the afternoon, so all parameters for severe weather were favorable, and both wind damage and hail were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail of 0.75 inches in diameter was observed for a few minutes.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief but strong EF-0 tornado occurred during the early morning hours of Sunday May 4, 2025 as a line of storms moved through central North Carolina. Several weakened trees on the property were snapped and one was uprooted. The tornado was on the ground for less than a minute before lifting.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado touched down in the Southern Terrace area of Princeville, NC, during the afternoon hours on Monday May 12, 2025, and traveled north into a farm field in Tarboro. The tornado then continued north along Wooten Street before dissipating near Elm Street.

Storms merged with an inland penetrating sea-breeze, leading to several flash flooding reports in Moore and Stanly Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding was reported at apartments along Southeast Service Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak disturbance out of South Carolina brought a batch of showers and storms into the Sandhills and Coastal Plain of central North Carolina during the afternoon. This led to a few storms producing wind damage in Cumberland county. Additionally, a stalled front over the Piedmont produced isolated storms in the late evening hours, which produced some large hail and wind damage in Stanly County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter to half dollar size hail was observed. Additionally, a tree was blown down in a yard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southward moving cold front out of Virginia stalled out near the North Carolina border. Storms from the late evening on the 15th persisted into the early morning hours of the 16th along and south of the front, producing isolated flash flooding. The stalled boundary then fueled additional numerous showers and storms in the afternoon and evening hours of the 16th along small scale boundaries. Several downed trees and flash flooding was reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Old Smithfield Road at Friday Road was closed due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front swept through the southern Appalachian region on April 6th, exiting the area to the east during the morning hours on April 7th. This front produced several hours of moderate to heavy rainfall in the mountains of east Tennessee and western North Carolina. This rainfall caused flooding along Tusquittee Creek near Hayesville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Stamey Cove Road was washed out earlier this morning by the flooded Tusquittee Creek. Water approached at least one house, flooding the front yard. Tusquittee Creek Road is closed along with a reported 7 other roads in Clay County. Creek gauge near Hayesville crested at 19.8 feet at 8:50 AM. Pictures shared via Facebook show Pine Log Creek has also escaped its banks and flooded backyards and low-lying lands along the creek. Water appears to be near at least one house in the photo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of heavy rain with embedded thunderstorms developed over the North Carolina Piedmont in association with a surface low and stalled frontal boundary draped over the Coastal Plain. Localized very heavy rainfall resulted in urban and small stream flash flooding in south Charlotte.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager and stream gauges reported flash flooding developed in south Charlotte, mainly along Little Sugar Creek and Little Hope Creek after 3 to 4 inches of rain fell in just a couple of hours. Little Hope Creek overflowed its banks and inundated part of Mockingbird Lane. Little Sugar Creek flooded a portion of Wakefield Dr, covered a part of Reece Rd with a couple of feet of water, and approached some homes south of Archdale Dr. Emergency manager reported multiple swift water rescues of motorists in south Charlotte. Media reported multiple cars stranded in floodwater in the Pineville area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front crossed the Appalachian Mountains on March 5. Strong winds aloft were mixed down to the surface from showers and thunderstorms, which caused notable reports of damaging winds that blew down numerous trees and power lines. The most notable damage reported was a roof and a metal carport blown down by the thunderstorm winds in Stokes County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds blew down one tree on to North Carolina Highway 16 near the Central Wilkes Middle School and one tree on to West Meadows Road about a half of a mile east of North Carolina Highway 16.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Within cool northeasterly surface flow, several upper-level disturbances tracked across central North Carolina from a persistent weak trough of low pressure over the Ohio Valley region. Copious amounts of moisture remained from the 5th of August. A wedge front was also in place along Interstate 95. Several reports of flash flooding were reported over the eastern Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain, including two fatalities in Nash County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two people died after their vehicle was swept off North Carolina Highway 581 and into a ravine or ditch that was overflowing with fast moving flood waters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very strong S/SE winds developed across the North Carolina mountains early in the morning in advance of a dynamic frontal system. The strongest winds occurred between 3 AM and 5 AM, possibly assisted by a band of rain with embedded heavy showers and isolated thunderstorms that mixed higher winds from aloft to the valley floors. Some minor structural damage was reported to houses across the region, while numerous trees were blown down, some onto structures, vehicles, and power lines. One tree fell on a trailer in the Conestee community of Transylvania County, killing a 13-year-old male and an 11-year-old male who were sleeping inside. Multiple outbuildings were damaged or destroyed in Haywood County. Power outages numbered in the tens of thousands at the peak of the event. The highest reliable measured gust across the area was at the Asheville Regional Airport, where official NWS obs measured a gust of 59 mph at 422 AM. However, damage reports suggest gusts likely reached as high as 70 mph in some locations. The band of showers and storms strengthened as it moved into the Piedmont later in the morning, with a small area of damaging wind gusts developing in northeast Union County in association with a short line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported (via social media) a couple of trees blown down northeast of Unionville.

The tide gauge at Duck, NC recorded major tidal flooding of 7.04 feet MLLW at 5:42 PM EST on August 21. Moderate flooding of 6.17 feet MLLW was observed at 6:36 PM EST on August 22.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding was reported at Indian Mound Road and Alpine Road. There were numerous other reports of flooded roads in the area east of US Highway 52 to Lake Tillery, south of Stony Gap Road and Highway 24/27.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper trough approached the Mid-Atlantic region from the west on June 19th. Strong solar heating and rich low level moisture combined for robust instability across the area. Moderate wind shear ahead of the upper trough resulted in sufficient shear for thunderstorm organization. A line of storms crossed into northeast North Carolina in the evening, producing scattered instances of wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported four trees and one powerline knocked down. They also reported power went out for the entire town of Murfreesboro.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread showers and embedded thunderstorms developed across the North Carolina Piedmont during the morning in the vicinity of a weak frontal boundary. An area of flooding developed across southern Rowan County in response to 2.5 to 4 inches of rain falling over several hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported stream flooding developed in areas south of Rockwell after 2.5 to 4 inches of rain fell across the area over a period of 4 to 6 hours. Klums Creek overflowed its banks and inundated Old Beatty Ford Rd. Water from a tributary inundated another portion of Old Beatty Ford near Emanual Church Rd. Another tributary overflowed onto Gin Rd near Eller Rd. Water also reportedly covered other roads in the area.

Flood advisories were also issued, with the main one being over Raleigh. After multiple days of above normal rainfall, including that which produced considerable flooding in Moore county and Chapel Hill, this additional rain led to flash flooding in the usual spots in Raleigh.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In a warm and humid air mass with weak steering flow but high moisture and instability, a few clusters of storms that started over the northwest Piedmont became more numerous as they tracked east southeast and approached the Triangle, producing areas of strong downdrafts and prompting three severe warnings over and southeast of the Triangle. Flood advisories were also issued, with the main one being over Raleigh. After multiple days of above normal rainfall, including that which produced considerable flooding in Moore county and Chapel Hill, this additional rain led to flash flooding in the usual spots in Raleigh.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few hundred power outages were reported, due to trees down on power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered slow-moving thunderstorms moved across the North Carolina mountains during the overnight and early morning hours. Localized torrential rainfall resulted in flash flooding across part of Jackson County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported flash flooding developed across a small part of northwest Jackson county after 2 to 3 inches of rain fell in less than two hours. The primary impact was to small streams and tributaries west of Thomas Valley Rd, where an unnamed stream inundated and washed out a bridge and a part of the Great Smoky Mountains Railroad. Additionally, Bumgarner Branch overflowed its banks and was rerouted into the yard of a home, with an occupant of the home requiring rescue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Chantal made landfall over northeastern South Carolina during the morning hours of July 6. The remnants of Chantal then tracked west-northwest into portions of central North Carolina, stalling out over the area before tracking east-northeast into Virginia by the 7th of July. Catastrophic flash flooding occurred from record rainfall of up to 11 inches in some spots of the Piedmont, included 6 flash flood fatalities across Chatham, Alamance, and Orange Counties. Widespread flooding particularly affected the counties of Orange, Chatman, and Moore. Four EF-1 tornadoes also touched down over portions Lee, Chatham, Alamance, and Orange Counties. Preliminary loss estimates across central North Carolina exceeded 40 million.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Aberdeen Creek flooded parts of North Carolina Highway 5 and US Highway 1 with several roads closed in the area. Damage estimates may have exceeded 5 million, including to roads, bridges, infrastructure, and residential areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In a warm and humid air mass with weak steering flow but high moisture and instability, a few clusters of storms that started over the northwest Piedmont became more numerous as they tracked east southeast and approached the Triangle, producing areas of strong downdrafts and prompting three severe warnings over and southeast of the Triangle. Catastrophic flash flooding occurred from record rainfall of up to 11 inches in some spots of the Piedmont, included 6 flash flood fatalities across Chatham, Alamance, and Orange Counties. Widespread flooding particularly affected the counties of Orange, Chatman, and Moore. Four EF-1 tornadoes also touched down over portions Lee, Chatham, Alamance, and Orange Counties. Preliminary loss estimates across central North Carolina exceeded 40 million.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Houses were flooded with stranded vehicles reported near Route 501 and South Elliott Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A hot and humid air mass combined with orographical lift to produce a severe thunderstorm in Surry County of northwest North Carolina. Damaging wind gusts from this storm blew down one tree and one power line.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds blew down one tree near the intersection of Siloam Road and Turkey Ford Road and one power line about one mile southeast of Dobson.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heat indices ranged from 108 to 112 degrees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms and storm clusters developed across the North Carolina foothills and western Piedmont during the afternoon and evening in association with a stationary front. Several storms produced severe weather in the form of locally damaging wind gusts. Additionally, several strong storms trained over the same locations in central McDowell County, resulting in flash flooding in the Marion area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported flash flooding developed in Marion and vicinity after 2.5 to 4 inches of rain fell in less than two hours. Flash flooding was first reported in downtown Marion, mainly in the form of  severe urban/drainage flooding. Two buildings were inundated and damaged: one on Henderson St and another on Court St. Youngs Fork overflowed its banks in Marion and overtopped the bridge on Shop Dr. A motorist was rescued on Owl Hollow Rd due to inundation from Jacktown Creek. The most significant impacts occurred at a campground along North Muddy Creek and Bledsoe Branch, where floodwater resulted in three swift water rescues, and evacuation of numerous additional people. Three buildings and multiple recreational and standard vehicles were flooded at this location.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Carson Street in Pilot Mountain, NC is was observed flooded around 1 foot deep as runoff from heavy rain overflowed a drainage ditch across the roadway, making the road impassible to traffic.  The road was reopened to traffic after the water receded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds occurred after the passage of a strong cold front as a pressure gradient increased between a departing low pressure system and a building high pressure system. Gusts of roughly 60 to 70 mph were measured by equipment across the northwest mountains of North Carolina between the late afternoon on the 29th through the pre-dawn hours of the 30th. The strongest measured gust, 71 mph, occurred near Blowing Rock in Watauga County late in the evening on the 29th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Winds gusted between 59 and 71 mph occurred across parts of Watauga County from the afternoon on the 29th through the early morning hours on the 30th. The strongest gusts were concentrated around the areas of Boone and Blowing Rock.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front crossed the region during the early morning hours of the 19th. Behind this front, strong to damaging west to northwest winds were reported, some of which blew down trees. The strongest reported wind gusts occurred in Watauga County, where a mesonet instrument measured 73 mph near Meat Camp. In Ashe County, a 67 mph gust was recorded by the AWOS at the Ashe County Airport (KGEV), and a 69 mph gust was measured near West Jefferson by a mesonet station.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mesonet site located one mile east of Piney Creek measured a wind gust of 60 mph at 8:04 AM EST.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 69 mph wind gust was reported by mesonet equipment located one mile north-northeast of West Jefferson at 11:30 AM EST. The high winds also caused a tree to be blown over onto a vehicle along Whenlin Ridge Road, one mile east of Flatwood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Erin made its closest approach to the North Carolina coast during the morning hours of Thursday, August 21st, 2025 as a category 2. While the center of Erin remained around 200 miles east of Cape Hatteras, Erin was so large that damaging ocean overwash and storm surge impacted Hatteras and Ocracoke Islands, and caused additional minor ocean overwash along ocean areas to the north and to the south, and minor soundside flooding on Hatteras and Ocracoke Islands, as well as Downeast Carteret County. According to the National Hurricane Center, Erin was one of the largest hurricanes on record. Additional impacts included dangerous rip currents on Eastern NC beaches, and tropical storm force gusts along the Outer Banks. Erin brought no rainfall or tornado impacts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Major overwash and storm surge significantly impacted Ocracoke Island for several days. A mandatory evacuation was issued for visitors and residents days before the main effects. While some overwash began on August 19th with distant swells, it became substantial on August 20th. Highway 12 on Ocracoke Island experienced severe inundation from ocean overwash and storm surge for several days, leading to beach erosion that exposed the sides of the road, as reported by NCDOT. The section of Highway 12 between the pony pens and the Ocracoke-Hatteras ferry terminal remained closed until 5:00 PM on Monday, August 25th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Erin made its closest approach to the North Carolina coast during the morning hours of Thursday, August 21st, 2025 as a category 2. While the center of Erin remained around 200 miles east of Cape Hatteras, Erin was so large that damaging ocean overwash and storm surge impacted Hatteras and Ocracoke Islands, and caused additional minor ocean overwash along ocean areas to the north and to the south, and minor soundside flooding on Hatteras and Ocracoke Islands, as well as Downeast Carteret County. According to the National Hurricane Center, Erin was one of the largest hurricanes on record. Additional impacts included dangerous rip currents on Eastern NC beaches, and tropical storm force gusts along the Outer Banks. Erin brought no rainfall or tornado impacts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Major ocean overwash and surge occurred for several days on Hatteras Island. Hatteras Island was under a mandatory evacuation for visitors and residents several days before significant impacts were noted. Some overwash occurred during the high tide cycle on the afternoon of August 19th as distant swell began impacting the Outer Banks. As the storm moved closer, overwash became significant on August 20th, and completely inundated Highway 12 in several sections on Hatteras Island for several days. Areas that became impassable due to severe ocean overwash include near Hatteras Village, Buxton, and the Pea Island Visitor Center area. Highway 12 on Hatteras Island did not fully reopen until noon on Saturday, August 23rd. The surge and overwash peaked on August 21st, as Erin made her closest approach to Cape Hatteras. Damages sustained to properties during the storm were primarily due to storm surge and ocean overwash. The damage was localized to the districts of Rodanthe and Buxton primarily along the oceanfront, with Buxton sustaining the more substantial damage. In Buxton, preliminary damage assessments from the county found damage to 56 residential structures and 4 commercial structures including driveways, parking lots, as well as septic systems and pipes. It should be noted that some minor sound side flooding also Occurred on Hatteras Island due to the northerly tropical storm force winds on the morning of August 21st, but no significant impacts occurred on the sound side.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A coastal low formed off of the Southeast coast on October 11 and slowly tracked north into October 13 before moving offshore. A large area of light to moderate rain moved into central North Carolina during the evening of the 18 December. This rain moved out during the overnight hours. As the cold front advanced eastward, a narrow line of storms tracked east from the Piedmont and Triad into the Triangle and northern Coastal Plain, before clearing out during the mid-morning hours. Several trees and powerlines were reported down across Randolph, Stanly, Chatham, Moore, Alamance, Orange, and Wake Counties. One tree fell through a roof of a home, but no injuries were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down across Love Mill Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An early season arctic front swept through the southern Appalachians late on the 9th, with snow levels falling quickly in the front's wake throughout the early morning of the 10th. The cold air interacted with moisture banked against the western slopes in northwest upslope flow to produce numerous snow showers that moved across mainly the Tennessee border counties throughout the 10th into the early morning of the 11th, resulting in the first notable snowfall of the season. Accumulations below about 3500 feet were generally in the 1-3 range, with some higher amounts along the Tennessee border. The higher elevations along the state line saw 5-10 with locally higher amounts of a foot or more on the high peaks.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NA

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An early season arctic front swept through the southern Appalachians late on the 9th, with snow levels falling quickly in the front's wake throughout the early morning of the 10th. The cold air interacted with moisture banked against the western slopes in northwest upslope flow to produce numerous snow showers that moved across mainly the Tennessee border counties throughout the 10th into the early morning of the 11th, resulting in the first notable snowfall of the season. Accumulations below about 3500 feet were generally in the 1-3 range, with some higher amounts along the Tennessee border. The higher elevations along the state line saw 5-10 with locally higher amounts of a foot or more on the high peaks.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NA

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Distant Hurricanes Humberto Imelda moved well off the East Coast at the end of the month, but produced major ocean overwash and wave runup affecting Hatteras and Ocracoke Islands for several days at the end of the month and into the beginning of October due to large long period swells. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure brought gusty winds to coastal portions of the northeast North Carolina Outer Banks September 15 into 16. On September 15, the low pressure system was located offshore and southeast of the area, with brief gusty winds to around 45 mph along the immediate coast in the afternoon due to a tightening pressure gradient. Wind gusts dropped below 40 mph from the evening into the early morning hours of September 16. However, winds increased and peaked in the morning and early afternoon September 16 as the low tracked northwest into the lower Chesapeake Bay and eventually moved inland. Peak wind gusts of around 50 mph were observed in coastal Currituck County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Increasingly gusty winds developed as a compact, but deepening, low pressure system approached the Virginia coast September 15 into 16. A brief period of wind gusts to around 45 mph occurred along the immediate Currituck County coast in the afternoon of September 15. Occasional wind gusts over 45 mph started in the early morning hours of September 16 and lasted through the early afternoon. A peak wind gust of 48 mph (42 kt) was observed at the Carova Beach Fire Department. Winds quickly decreased later in the later afternoon and evening.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms and small storm clusters developed across the North Carolina Piedmont during the evening. Several of these clusters moved over south Charlotte, where multiple storms moved repeatedly over the same locations. Very heavy rainfall and significant flash flooding resulted. One of the storms also produced hail over Charlotte.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Stream gauges and the media reported flash flooding developed across south Charlotte after 2.5 to 5 inches of rain fell across the area due to slow-moving, repeating thunderstorms. Most of the major streams in this part of the city overflowed their banks and inundated adjacent roads, greenways, and residential yards, including Little Hope Creek, Edwards Branch, and Little Sugar Creek. The most significant flooding occurred along Steele Creek in the Steele Creek community, which inundated a mobile home park. Multiple manufactured homes were inundated in this area, and multiple vehicles were largely subsumed in water. Around 30 swift water rescues occurred throughout the city during the event, with most of these occurring in the mobile home park. Thirteen people were also rescued from their vehicles near Freedom Park (Little Sugar Creek). McMullen Creek also experienced severe flooding, with water entering the crawl spaces of some homes and cutting off access to others.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation associated with an intensifying low pressure system over the Deep South developed across the North Carolina mountains during the evening of the 24th, beginning as a mix of sleet and snow. Increasing southwest winds overnight resulted in steadily warming temperatures allowing the precipitation to change to freezing rain and rain across the Smokies and vicinity by daybreak. By mid-morning, precip had changed to rain across the entire area. Total sleet and snow accumulations generally ranged from one tenth to around one half inch. Some high elevation locations as well as some locations in the upper Tuckasegee and upper Pigeon valleys also saw a few hundredths of an inch of ice accretion.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NA

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful winter storm developed on 24 January and did not fully let up until early on 26 January. After a strong Arctic cold front arrived the prior day, an area of low pressure tracked across the southeastern United States, bringing a plume of moisture into the Carolinas. A wintry mix of freezing rain, sleet, and snow developed, with the greatest snow and sleet accumulations over the Piedmont and the highest ice accumulations over the Sandhills and Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A half inch to an inch of snow and sleet fell across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation associated with an intensifying low pressure system over the Deep South developed across the southern North Carolina foothills around midnight early on the 25th. The precipitation began as mostly sleet, which continued through the early morning hours before mixing with, and eventually changing to freezing rain later in the morning. The precipitation finally tapered off during the early evening. Total sleet accumulations of 1 to 2 inches occurred, with around 0.25 inch of ice accreting on top of the sleet. This made for very hazardous driving conditions. Due to unusually cold weather following the event, several days of refreezing resulted in travel difficulties continuing during the overnight and morning hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NA

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure area with a cold front attached to it tracked east across the Carolinas during the late morning and afternoon timeframe. Along and and out ahead of the cold front a line of scattered to numerous severe thunderstorms developed and quickly raced east northeast across Eastern NC, producing 60 to 70 mph wind gusts. With ample instability and strong wind shear in place several of the storms interacted with the sea breeze inland from the coast and produced several tornadoes, in addition to severe thunderstorm wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of trees blown down in Bear Grass.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent upper-level low tracked south and then southeast from the Upper Midwest to the Southeast during the weekend of Friday January 30th to Sunday February 1st. At the same time, a baroclinic zone set up along the offshore waters of Georgia, westwards to the Deep South. A surface low then developed along this baroclinic zone just off the coast of Georgia during the early morning hours on Saturday January 31st. As the upper level low neared the developing surface low, this resulted in a Miller-A low pressure system. The associated offshore low pressure system then rapidly strengthened as it tracked northeastwards just off the North Carolina coast during the overnight hours between Saturday and Sunday. This very strong low then pulled away from the Carolinas and moved out into the open waters of the North Atlantic during the late morning hours on Sunday. With an unusually cold airmass in place across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, a rather widespread and historic snowstorm for almost all of Eastern North Carolina occurred. Snow began during the morning hours on Saturday January 31st mainly along the Crystal Coast and Inner Banks, though a period of light snow occurred across portions of the Coastal Plain as well Saturday morning. By Saturday afternoon the low pressure system off the coast began to deepen quickly resulting in heavier and more widespread snowfall across much of Eastern North Carolina. Snowfall rates became heavy at times resulting in periods of whiteout conditions as 30-50 mph wind gusts (60-65 mph on the Outer Banks) also impacted the area making travel treacherous across the region. Snow finally pushed completely offshore by the late morning hours on Sunday February 1st. Over 10 inches of snowfall were measured across most counties of Eastern North Carolina outside of Hatteras Island and Ocracoke with several counties reporting over a foot of snowfall. The strong winds associated with the low also produced coastal flooding on the Outer Banks of Hatteras and Ocracoke Islands. Highway 12 was closed for a time, and 4 more homes in the Buxton area collapsed into the ocean due to the coastal flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snowfall reports from the public and CoCoRaHs data showed between six and thirteen inches of snowfall fell across Martin County between the morning of January thirty-first and the morning of February first.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong northwest winds pushing colder air into the area in the wake of an arctic cold front interacting with moisture banked against the western slopes of the Appalachians resulted in a protracted period of snow showers developing near the Tennessee/North Carolina border. The snow showers began developing on the morning of the 22nd, and continued off and on for more than 36 hours before tapering off during the early morning of the 24th. Snowfall totals were heavily dependent upon elevation and exposure to northwest winds, with general amounts of 4-8 inches reported above 3500 feet. Locally higher amounts of 10 inches or more occurred on the high peaks along the Tennessee border. Much ligheter amounts occurred in the valleys, with less than an inch reported in the valleys beneath the Smokies, to as much as 4 inches in the higher valleys of the northern mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NA

By Saturday afternoon the low pressure system off the coast began to deepen quickly resulting in heavier and more widespread snowfall across much of Eastern North Carolina. Snowfall rates became heavy at times resulting in periods of whiteout conditions as 30-50 mph wind gusts (60-65 mph on the Outer Banks) also impacted the area making travel treacherous across the region. Snow finally pushed completely offshore by the late morning hours on Sunday February 1st. Over 10 inches of snowfall were measured across most counties of Eastern North Carolina outside of Hatteras Island and Ocracoke with several counties reporting over a foot of snowfall. The strong winds associated with the low also produced coastal flooding on the Outer Banks of Hatteras and Ocracoke Islands. Highway 12 was closed for a time, and 4 more homes in the Buxton area collapsed into the ocean due to the coastal flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful winter storm developed on 24 January and did not fully let up until early on 26 January. After a strong Arctic cold front arrived the prior day, an area of low pressure tracked across the southeastern United States, bringing a plume of moisture into the Carolinas. A wintry mix of freezing rain, sleet, and snow developed, with the greatest snow and sleet accumulations over the Piedmont and the highest ice accumulations over the Sandhills and Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One to two inches of snow and sleet fell across the county, with also up to a tenth of an inch of freezing rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper trough moved through the region in early February, spawning deepening surface low pressure offshore. A very steep pressure gradient resulted in strong winds across northeast North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Weatherstem sensor at Jarvisburg Elementary School experienced strong winds as low pressure deepened offshore. Sustained winds were above 40 mph from 2:30-3:30 AM EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper trough moved through the region in early February, spawning deepening surface low pressure offshore. A very steep pressure gradient resulted in strong winds across northeast North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The C-MAN sensor at Duck Pier experienced strong winds as low pressure deepened offshore. Sustained winds were above 40 mph from midnight until 8:00 AM EST. Winds gusted above 40 mph from midnight through early afternoon with a peak gust of 59 mph measured at 6:42 AM EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper low and subsequent coastal low pressure brought strong winds and cold temperatures to the region in early February.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Weatherstem sensor at Jarvisburg Elementary School in Jarvisburg, NC recorded a wind chill of -2 degrees F at 9:20 AM EST on February 1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions were introduced across the North Carolina and Virginia Piedmonts in early January after the previous two months of November and December recorded precipitation totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, which ended up being 25 to 50 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November and December, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd to 5th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 6th of January. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions were introduced to Caswell county in early January after the previous two months of November and December recorded precipitation totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, which ended up being 25 to 50 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November and December,  contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 5th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 6th of January. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Dan River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent upper-level low tracked south and then southeast from the Upper Midwest to the Southeast during the weekend of Friday January 30th to Sunday February 1st. At the same time, a baroclinic zone set up along the offshore waters of Georgia, westwards to the Deep South. A surface low then developed along this baroclinic zone just off the coast of Georgia during the early morning hours on Saturday. As the upper level low neared the developing surface low, this resulted in a Miller-A low pressure system. The associated offshore low pressure system then rapidly deepened as it tracked northeastwards just off the North Carolina coast during the overnight hours between Saturday and Sunday. This very strong low then pulled away from the Carolinas and moved out into the open waters of the North Atlantic during the late morning hours on Sunday. With an unusually cold airmass in place across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, a rather widespread and historic snowstorm for almost all of Eastern North Carolina occurred. Snow began during the morning hours on Saturday mainly along the Crystal Coast and Inner Banks, though a period of light snow occurred across portions of the Coastal Plain as well Saturday morning. By Saturday afternoon the low pressure system off the coast began to deepen quickly resulting in heavier and more widespread snowfall across much of Eastern North Carolina. Snowfall rates became heavy at times resulting in periods of whiteout conditions as 30-50 mph wind gusts (60-65 mph on the Outer Banks) also impacted the area making travel treacherous across the region. Snow finally pushed completely offshore by the late morning hours on Sunday. Over 10 inches of snowfall were measured across most counties of Eastern North Carolina outside of Hatteras Island and Ocracoke with several counties reporting over a foot of snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread reports between public, CoCoRahs, trained spotters, and NWS employees of ten to nineteen inches of snowfall including fifteen inches of snowfall at the NWS Newport Morehead City office. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent upper-level low tracked south and then southeast from the Upper Midwest to the Southeast during the weekend of Friday January 30th to Sunday February 1st. At the same time, a baroclinic zone set up along the offshore waters of Georgia, westwards to the Deep South. A surface low then developed along this baroclinic zone just off the coast of Georgia during the early morning hours on Saturday. As the upper level low neared the developing surface low, this resulted in a Miller-A low pressure system. The associated offshore low pressure system then rapidly deepened as it tracked northeastwards just off the North Carolina coast during the overnight hours between Saturday and Sunday. This very strong low then pulled away from the Carolinas and moved out into the open waters of the North Atlantic during the late morning hours on Sunday. With an unusually cold airmass in place across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, a rather widespread and historic snowstorm for almost all of Eastern North Carolina occurred. Snow began during the morning hours on Saturday mainly along the Crystal Coast and Inner Banks, though a period of light snow occurred across portions of the Coastal Plain as well Saturday morning. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and transportation delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 3.0 inches of snow, up to 2.5 inches of sleet, and up to 0.01 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: power outages, transportation delays.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and transportation delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 3.5 inches of snow, up to 2.0 inches of sleet, and up to 0.05 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: power outages, transportation delays.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent upper-level low tracked south and then southeast from the Upper Midwest to the Southeast during the weekend of Friday January 30th to Sunday February 1st. At the same time, a baroclinic zone set up along the offshore waters of Georgia, westwards to the Deep South. A surface low then developed along this baroclinic zone just off the coast of Georgia during the early morning hours on Saturday. As the upper level low neared the developing surface low, this resulted in a Miller-A low pressure system. The associated offshore low pressure system then rapidly deepened as it tracked northeastwards just off the North Carolina coast during the overnight hours between Saturday and Sunday. This very strong low then pulled away from the Carolinas and moved out into the open waters of the North Atlantic during the late morning hours on Sunday. With an unusually cold airmass in place across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, a rather widespread and historic snowstorm for almost all of Eastern North Carolina occurred. Snow began during the morning hours on Saturday mainly along the Crystal Coast and Inner Banks, though a period of light snow occurred across portions of the Coastal Plain as well Saturday morning. By Saturday afternoon the low pressure system off the coast began to deepen quickly resulting in heavier and more widespread snowfall across much of Eastern North Carolina. Snowfall rates became heavy at times resulting in periods of whiteout conditions as 30-50 mph wind gusts (60-65 mph on the Outer Banks) also impacted the area making travel treacherous across the region. Snow finally pushed completely offshore by the late morning hours on Sunday. Over 10 inches of snowfall were measured across most counties of Eastern North Carolina outside of Hatteras Island and Ocracoke with several counties reporting over a foot of snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall reports from the public and COOP observers showed between six and ten inches of snowfall fell across Greene County between the morning of January thirty-first and the morning of February first.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and transportation delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 3.1 inches of snow, up to 2.6 inches of sleet, and up to 0.05 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: power outages, transportation delays.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions worsened across north central North Carolina, and Exceptional Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought in northwest North Carolina in the middle of June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, and locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 10 to 25 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 16th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple thunderstorm cells were observed training across the Flat Rock Community, located just northeast of the town of Mt Airy in Surry County. Cells began crossing the area at around 5:45 pm EDT, and continued passing across the area repeatedly until around 8:15 pm EDT before rainfall became light in intensity. Rainfall rates rose to as high as 5 inches per hour multiple times through the event. Despite dry antecedent conditions with D2: Severe Drought highlighted for the northern half of Surry County by the U.S. Drought Monitor, MRMS FLASH data estimated the rainfall reached the 142-year Average Recurrence Interval ceiling for a 3-hour duration in the Flat Rock area, with rainfall totals reaching 120 percent of the 3-hour Flash Flood Guidance. CREST Unit Streamflow was unimpressive however, reaching into the 300 to 400 cfs per mi^2 by around 8:00 pm EDT. The heavy rain produced runoff around 6 inches deep across Highway 103 from a nearby hillside drainage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Runoff from heavy rain was observed flowing across Highway 103 around 6 inches deep. No damage was observed to the road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions worsened across north central North Carolina, and Exceptional Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought in northwest North Carolina in the middle of June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, and locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 10 to 25 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 16th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Exceptional Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought conditions in Ashe county through the end of June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 10.00-15.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, and January, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 10th to 20th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the New River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms developed across the North Carolina Piedmont during the morning in advance of a cold front. The relative slow movement of the cluster resulted in heavy-to-torrential rainfall that continued for a couple of hours along the Mecklenburg/Union County line, with flash flooding developing across northern Union County.

Flooding of a parking lot adjacent to the intersection of Indian Trail Fairview Rd and Idlewild Rd was reported and a small portion of Indian Trail Fairview Rd was closed as a result. The lower level of a home flooded near the intersection of White Oak Ln and Cupped Oak Dr, as did the intersection itself. Other roads reported to have flooded included Lawyers Rd at N Rocky River Rd and Oak Spring Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of western North Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. The dry and warm conditions enhanced the wildfire danger across the region, but large wildfires were few and far between, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was initiated in late March. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wrightsville Beach Ocean Rescue performed a four person rip current rescue Thursday evening. One woman pulled from the water was not breathing and was able to be resuscitated. They recovered in the hospital over the next couple of days.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across north central and northwest North Carolina in early and late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21th of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows. A couple snowfall events in late February contributed to some relief in streamflows and areawide drought conditions; however, precipitation totals still fell short, and overall lead to some minor Severe Drought Expansions across the area.

This included the Dan River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed across western North Carolina during the afternoon and evening. A series of thunderstorm cells became anchored on the slopes of Bearwallow Mountain in Henderson County, resulting in torrential rainfall that lasted for a couple of hours, resulting in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple sources reported significant flash flooding developed across northeast Henderson County after 4 to 7 inches of rain fell on the slopes of Bearwallow Mountain in just a couple of hours. The main impact was to Clear Creek and its tributaries, including Puncheon Camp Creek, Cox Creek, and Laurel Fork. A culvert washed out underneath a section of Highway 74 in the Gerton community, forcing closure of the road for a few days. A section of Bearwallow Rd was also washed out in the Edneyville area. Multiple other roads were inundated and closed throughout the area, while multiple culverts under private driveways and some small bridges were reportedly washed out or damaged. A few homes were briefly isolated due to washed out culverts or flooded roads. The high flows on Clear Creek, combined with subsequent heavy rainfall in the Mud Creek basin resulted in the French Broad River rising to bankfull in Flecther and vicinity.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: In coordination with Pamlico County Emergency Management, a survey of damage along HWY 55 in Stonewall found damage consistent with straight line winds of 80 to 90 mph. In this area, a mobile home strapped down with hurricane ties was moved 3 to 4 feet off its foundation. The ties were ripped out of the ground. The home sustained damage to siding and windows. A nearby home on Spain Farm Road sustained minor damage to a patio and outdoor light fixtures. The time was estimated based on observer report and radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved slowly southward through the Mid-Atlantic, triggering scattered thunderstorms with heavy rainfall rates and severe weather. While shear was not very high (<30 knots), the atmosphere was considerably unstable with SBCAPE values of at least 2000 J/kg. Low level lapse rates and mid-level lapse rates were up to 8.5 C��/km and  6.5��C/km, respectively, in the Piedmont. All these parameters, combined with DCAPE values of 1000-1400 J/kg, resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms that reached as far south as North Carolina. One storm in particular sent a swath of trees and power lines down in Mount Airy of Surry County. This storm formed and intensified after crossing the Blue Ridge and shortly dissipated in Stokes County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A swath of trees were reported in the White Plains community at near I-74. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms that passed over the mountains earlier in the day reorganized and strengthened to become severe thunderstorms later in the evening in North Carolina. A few notable cells travelled west to east just south of the VA/NC border and brought numerous trees and power lines down. This part of the forecast area had notable deep moisture convergence and CAPE of about 1000-2000 J/kg. Lapse rates were underwhelming at the low level and mid-level, but bulk shear of 30-40 knots allowed sufficient storm organization and intensification to deliver several damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down off of Old County Home Road in the Dobson Community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in north-central North Carolina. A few swaths of damage were reported in the counties of Surry, Stokes, Rockingham, and Caswell with at least one report of a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was reported down by the intersection of CC Camp Road and Still Meadows Lane.

Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in north-central North Carolina. A few swaths of damage were reported in the counties of Surry, Stokes, Rockingham, and Caswell with at least one report of a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down at the 1100 Block of River Siloam Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved slowly southward through the Mid-Atlantic, triggering scattered thunderstorms with heavy rainfall rates and severe weather. While shear was not very high (<30 knots), the atmosphere was considerably unstable with SBCAPE values of at least 2000 J/kg. Low level lapse rates and mid-level lapse rates were up to 8.5 C��/km and  6.5��C/km, respectively, in the Piedmont. All these parameters, combined with DCAPE values of 1000-1400 J/kg, resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms that reached as far south as North Carolina. One storm in particular sent a swath of trees and power lines down in Mount Airy of Surry County. This storm formed and intensified after crossing the Blue Ridge and shortly dissipated in Stokes County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Five fallen tree reports. Two separate reports along Perry Taylor Road near Mt. Airy. Another tree was down near the intersection of McKinney Road and Old Hwy 601. The final two were also along McKinney Road.

Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. The dry and warm conditions enhanced the wildfire danger across the region, but large wildfires were few and far between, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was initiated in late March. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.
